summary: A minimum spanning tree (MST) of a connected, weighted, undirected graph is a set of V - 1 edges that connects all vertices with the smallest possible total weight and no cycles. Kruskal's and Prim's greedy algorithms both build one.

sections.heading: Why MSTs matter
bullets: Laying cable, pipes, or roads with minimum total cost.
Approximation algorithms (such as for the traveling salesman problem).

sections.heading: Kruskal's algorithm
sections.body: Sort all edges by weight. Scan them in increasing order and keep an edge if it connects two different components (checked with union-find); otherwise it would form a cycle. Stop after V - 1 edges.

sections.heading: Prim's algorithm
sections.body: Grow a single tree from any start vertex. Repeatedly add the cheapest edge that connects the tree to a vertex outside it. With a min-heap of candidate edges it runs in O(E log V); with an adjacency matrix and arrays, O(V²).

sections.heading: Complexity and choosing
bullets: Kruskal: O(E log E) from sorting; good for sparse graphs.
Prim with heap: O(E log V); Prim with arrays: O(V²), good for dense graphs.
Both produce a tree of the same total weight; with distinct weights the MST is unique.

sections.heading: Correctness: cut and cycle properties
sections.body: Cut property: for any partition of the vertices, the lightest edge crossing the cut belongs to some MST. Cycle property: the heaviest edge on any cycle is not in an MST (if its weight is strictly largest). Both greedy algorithms apply these rules repeatedly.
Edges: (A-B,1), (B-C,2), (A-C,3), (C-D,4), (B-D,5). Sorted: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Take A-B (1), B-C (2); A-C (3) would form a cycle, skip; take C-D (4). V - 1 = 3 edges, total weight 7.
Cycle detection is the bottleneck. Union-find with path compression and union by rank makes each check nearly O(1), so sorting dominates the running time.
If the graph is not connected, Kruskal naturally yields a spanning forest, one MST per component. Prim must be restarted from an unvisited vertex.

bullets: Second-best MST: swap one non-tree edge.
Bottleneck path: the MST path minimizes the largest edge.
Clustering: stop Kruskal at k components (single-linkage clustering).

sections.body: An MST minimizes total edge weight across the whole tree; a Dijkstra shortest-path tree minimizes the distance from one root to each vertex. They can differ.

takeaways: An MST connects all V vertices with V - 1 edges at minimum total weight.
Kruskal: sort edges, add if no cycle (union-find). Prim: grow one tree by the cheapest crossing edge.
O(E log E) for Kruskal, O(E log V) for heap-based Prim.
Cut and cycle properties justify the greedy choice.
